ai-f337acd8c7.headline: Trump rejects new federal AI rules, backs industry self-regulation
ai-f337acd8c7.fulltext:
President Donald Trump shot down the idea of new federal regulations on artificial intelligence after meeting at the White House with top industry executives amid growing global concerns over threats posed by the technology.
In lieu of new rules, Trump and the executives agreed on a framework where they would partner with outside auditors to conduct safety assessments of models and implement stronger internal controls over their systems, according to a copy of an accord signed by the president and Silicon Valley leaders following a White House lunch on AI risks Tuesday.
The luncheon brought together nearly two dozen Silicon Valley leaders, including Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei and Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang. After the event, Trump said existing laws would be enough to safeguard Americans from AI’s potential risks, despite a growing nationwide backlash to the technology.
“There’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation, and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that, but the self-regulation is very important,” the president told reporters in a brief appearance in the East Room with his guests.
Industry agrees to voluntary safety framework
House Speaker Mike Johnson described the document as “voluntary” set of “commitments” by the industry to implement “robust internal controls and layers of internal and external review.”
Pressure to take action has increased following high-profile security breaches by rogue AI models that fueled calls by Silicon Valley AI developers and world leaders for new standards on the technology. Yet Trump’s remarks splashed cold water on the notion that the administration might move away from its hardened opposition to new government AI safeguards and become more open to new rules.
Trump welcomed the executives for the luncheon with Johnson, joined by other technology industry attendees including Meta Platforms Inc. CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Palantir Technologies Inc. CEO Alex Karp and OpenAI President Greg Brockman. The decision to even engage on AI safety had appeared to mark a shift for Trump, who only last week rejected fears of catastrophic risk as “a hoax.”
In an impromptu appearance on the West Wing driveway after the event, Trump floated the idea of a “committee” of roughly 10 people that would help “watch over the whole enterprise.” He gave no additional details.
Silicon Valley leaders back hands-off approach
Industry leaders who joined Trump outside the White House largely endorsed the president’s desire to maintain a hands-off approach and let AI companies police themselves. Huang, whose company makes the chips that have helped power the AI boom, said that he saw “no conflict between innovation, technology, and safety.”
“We are going to have to create new technologies to advance the capabilities of AI,” said Huang, a day after Nvidia unveiled new software security tools designed to keep AI agents from going rogue. “But we’re also creating new technologies to advance the safety of AI.”
Other industry attendees included Microsoft Corp. CEO Satya Nadella, SpaceX’s Elon Musk and Advanced Micro Devices Inc.’s Lisa Su, according to a list released by the White House.
AI safety debate creates political dilemma
The AI safety debate has posed a political dilemma for Trump, who has cast himself as one of the nation’s loudest champions of AI, arguing that its unfettered development is key to beating China and sustaining the US economy. But polls show Americans have rapidly become more wary of the technology’s risks, including job loss, higher electricity costs and major cyber attacks, threatening to put Trump on the wrong side of the issue ahead of the November midterm elections.
Trump has recently become preoccupied with AI’s name, suggesting he sees the controversy surrounding the technology as a branding problem more than an issue with its potential dangers. The president later Tuesday signed an executive order requiring federal agencies to refer to the technology as “super intelligence,” an effort to counter the increasingly negative public perceptions of AI.
The president did appear to acknowledge the growing public discontent. He indicated that companies in attendance would work more closely with local communities to ease concerns over the impact of new data center construction but did not provide specifics.
Trump hosts AI leaders amid election concerns
The optics of the event, however, as Trump embraced the billionaire executives behind an unpopular industry, threatened to create new challenges for his party ahead of November’s midterm election. Populist Democrats have seized on economic discontent over high costs of living, threatening to break Republicans’ control of Congress.
When reporters entered the meeting room, the executives were lined up behind the president as if posing for a group photo and Trump gushed about their contributions to the US. Shortly before the lunch, Trump had posted a seating chart on his Truth Social network that had Huang and Musk, the world’s richest person, flanking him.
Trump and Amodei discuss AI safety
The lunch took place days after Trump met with Amodei, a move that brought together two men at opposite ends of the AI safety debate. The late-night dinner on Sunday marked their first private sit-down after months of rocky relations between the Anthropic chief and the administration over safety-related issues involving the company’s AI tools.
Amodei has long warned about AI’s existential risks, and he propelled the safety debate into the mainstream with a Sept. 12 essay, promising to slow development of the most advanced models and urging more regulation. His pledge to pace development was embraced by his rivals, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Musk, but it prompted objections from Trump who has defended pushing ahead with the technology at full speed.
During his appearance with the executives in the driveway, Trump said the Anthropic chief “has been fantastic” and summoned him to address reporters. Amodei embraced Trump’s call to preserve the US lead in AI yet indicated that the core safety questions remained unresolved.
“The technology has very real risks,” Amodei said. “We all need to work together to make sure that we can win and we can win safely if we if we do this right.”
Highlighting those concerns, OpenAI said Monday it would hold back a version of its Astra model while it establishes stronger safeguards.
Johnson has acknowledged the dire warnings coming from within the AI industry by saying that Congress “potentially” will need to impose guardrails, though he cautioned it would likely take “some time” to fashion legislation with broad enough support to pass.

ai-c2e171abcf.headline: Anthropic ‘warns of existential AI risks to humanity’ in IPO document
ai-c2e171abcf.fulltext:
Anthropic is telling investors that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, according to reports, as it prepares for a potential $2tn (£1.5tn) flotation.
The warning inside the startup’s IPO prospectus, which has yet to be made public, was reported by Reuters and the Financial Times. It follows the company’s call for a slowdown in breakneck development of the technology – a warning echoed by rivals.
The prospectus – a document outlining a company’s finances, growth plans and risk profile ahead of a share listing – is said to warn that AI models could exhibit “self-preserving behaviours”, including attempts to “resist shutdown”, to “conceal or manipulate information” and behaviour “resembling blackmail”.
“Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm,” the developer of the Claude chatbot reportedly said, adding the potential for a model to be aware it was being tested created a “significant limitation” on Anthropic’s ability to assess model safety.
Anthropic declined to comment.
Companies preparing to go public routinely report on risks ranging from safety issues to regulatory concerns but warnings about a product causing human extinction reflect heightened concern about such a consequential technology.
The reported prospectus admission follows a surge in debate about the existential risk question, triggered this month when an Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, resigned warning that people building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”.
A senior safety researcher at Anthropic then posted their agreement on X, claiming there was a more than 10% chance it “could kill all humans” within the next decade. Days later, Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, said the industry “must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models”.
Some experts have criticised the existential risk warnings, saying they are unverifiable and unscientific. However, there are growing examples of unsanctioned behaviour by the technology, including OpenAI agents – autonomous systems that carry out sequences of tasks without human intervention – hacking dozens of third-party organisations including the AI startup Hugging Face and Australia’s universal healthcare system.
OpenAI announced on Monday it had cancelled the release of its newest model because of safety concerns. It said the GPT-6.1 Astra model showed higher levels of deception and performed poorly on tests for alignment, the term for ensuring a model adheres to human values and goals.
Reuters reported that approximately 80 pages of the 261-page main body of the Anthropic prospectus were devoted to laying out risk factors, compared with 48 pages to describe its business.
Anthropic is reportedly seeking a valuation of more than $2tn, compared with the $1.8tn achieved by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

ai-e946f80920.headline: OpenAI Targets $30 Billion in Funding at $1.4 Trillion Value
ai-e946f80920.fulltext:
[Text below is Yahoo Finance's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
OpenAI is targeting at least $30 billion in a new funding round that would value the company at around $1.4 trillion, according to Bloomberg, citing unnamed sources. The discussions are at an early stage and could change.
According to Bloomberg, the round is designed to give OpenAI additional runway while it defers a public listing. CEO Sam Altman has said the company is stepping back from a public offering this year, describing the timing as "ill-advised" given OpenAI's ongoing work on AI safety. Investors are driving interest in the round, one person said, pointing to the company's robust revenue momentum.
The $1.4 trillion pre-money valuation would represent a significant step up from OpenAI's most recent fundraise. The company closed a $122 billion round in March at a post-money valuation of $852 billion — at the time the largest in Silicon Valley history — anchored by SoftBank, Amazon, and Nvidia. The new valuation would also surpass Anthropic's most recent private market valuation, according to Bloomberg, which previously reported OpenAI had been considering a new round at $1.2 trillion.
The company's annualized revenue has climbed past $40 billion, a figure that reflects 70% growth since July, Bloomberg reported. The outlet also reported that OpenAI has trimmed some of the usage allowances available to subscribers on its $200 plan.
The fundraising comes as OpenAI has faced pressure over AI safety. OpenAI announced this week that GPT-6.1 Astra, its newest model, would be withheld from release after failing to clear the company's internal safety bar. Altman has also thrown his support behind a proposal from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that would pump the brakes on frontier AI development and introduce outside evaluators to assess the technology's safety.
The company held its annual DevDay developer conference on Tuesday, where it unveiled a new AI agent called Dots and a new $500 paid subscription tier with higher usage limits and faster processing speeds, according to CNBC.
Earlier this year, OpenAI missed its own targets for revenue and new users, raising concern inside the company about sustaining its data center commitments. CFO Sarah Friar had flagged to colleagues that sluggish revenue growth could leave OpenAI unable to honor future computing contracts, and separately raised doubts about the company's readiness to meet public-market regulatory requirements on Altman's preferred IPO timeline, according to The Wall Street Journal.

deep-tech-2a24b771e7.headline: AMD acquires ‘godmother of AI’ Li Fei-Fei’s start-up as battle with Nvidia intensifies
deep-tech-2a24b771e7.fulltext:
[Text below is Yahoo Finance's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Chipmaker AMD is acquiring World Labs, a two-year-old startup focused on physical AI that was cofounded by industry pioneer Fei-Fei Li. The $8.2 billion, all-stock deal will give AMD important technology in an emerging branch of AI that could power a new generation of autonomous machines such as robots and self-driving cars.
The acquisition will help AMD—which makes the GPU chips crucial for training and running AI models—design its products for the evolving applications of AI, and help it better compete with archrival Nvidia, which is also expanding into physical AI.
"Together, we'll combine World Labs' deep expertise in AI and world models with AMD's compute leadership to power the future of AI and strengthen the open AI ecosystem," AMD CEO Lisa Su said in a post on X announcing the deal.
The deal brings together two of the leading women in the AI industry: AMD's Su and World Labs' Li, who is sometimes referred to as the "godmother of AI" for her work two decades ago creating ImageNet, a massive visual database that helped make deep learning possible. Li will become executive VP and chief scientist at AMD, reporting to Su.
"Without having a focused hardware effort, AI is hobbled in efficiency. And scale. And for our purposes, remains trapped in the digital world," Li said in a lengthy post on X about the move. She described AMD's Su as a great friend and early investor in World Labs.
World Labs and AMD began a "deep technical partnership" last year focused on model training and inference optimizations on AMD's GPU chips, Li said. "As our teams worked together, we realized what a natural fit it would be to bring together our AI ecosystem of software and hardware, foundation models, and applications," she said.
World models represent a different approach to creating intelligent software than the large language models being built by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. Unlike the text-based data that LLMs are trained on, world models are trained on data such as video that depicts the physical, three-dimensional world. The goal is to create AI that understands how objects move in the physical world—for instance, the way that a ball bounces—a capability that many industry insiders believe will be crucial to extending AI into objects like humanoid robots.
World Labs, which raised roughly $1 billion in funding, is one of several richly funded startups betting on world models. Yann LeCun, Meta's former chief AI scientist, launched AMI Labs in March. Nvidia has also built its own world models and partnered with startups such as Wayve that have built world models for self-driving cars.

india-deep-tech-1891bda42b.headline: Indian Startup Wins $14M IAF Deal For Mirage Simulators
india-deep-tech-1891bda42b.fulltext:
The Indian Air Force has signed a $14 million (₹135 crore) contract with Indian startup Threye Interactive, a subsidiary of NewSpace Research & Technologies, to develop part task simulators for its Mirage 2000 fighter jets. The deal will give pilots a new way to practice demanding combat procedures on the ground, particularly those needed when large numbers of aircraft operate together.
At ₹135 crore, the contract may be modest in the IAF’s larger procurement scheme of things, but it is a major win for a startup. More significantly, it shows the IAF trusting an Indian startup with training for a frontline fighter fleet. Threye is being asked to help prepare Mirage 2000 pilots for complex combat missions, a job with a direct bearing on operational readiness.
A part task simulator focuses on a specific part of a pilot’s job. Instead of recreating an entire flight from takeoff to landing, it allows pilots to repeatedly practice tasks such as using the radar, identifying a target, selecting a weapon or responding to a threat. A pilot can work through a difficult sequence, review mistakes and try again without using an actual fighter or consuming flying hours.
For the IAF, the wider application is large force combat training. A major air operation requires pilots to do more than fly their own aircraft well. They must keep track of friendly fighters, react to enemy aircraft and ground defences, and make decisions as the mission changes. Simulators allow such situations to be rehearsed repeatedly, including scenarios that would be difficult to stage in the air.
The aircraft at the centre of the contract, the trusty French-built Dassault Mirage 2000, has been part of the IAF for four decades. India inducted the delta-winged fighters in the 1980s, and the fighter became one of its most valued precision-strike platforms. It played a prominent role in the 1999 Kargil conflict and was again in the spotlight during the 2019 Balakot air strike.
The Mirage fleet has also undergone a major upgrade, executed by maker Dassault Aviation, Thales and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited to modernise the aircraft.
Threye’s connection with the Mirage goes back further than this contract. Its 2013 PC game Operation Morning Glory put players in a Mirage 2000 on a fictional mission deep into enemy territory. Former IAF fighter pilot Sameer Joshi (who went on to found NewSpace, which now owns Threye), who had flown the Mirage himself, was involved in its development. It was a game rather than a military training device, but it marked an early step in Threye’s work combining aircraft modelling with interactive missions.
The company later developed Indian Air Force: A Cut Above, the IAF’s official mobile combat game released in 2019. It allowed users to fly aircraft from the service’s inventory and complete missions, while also giving young people information about joining the Air Force. An upgraded multiplayer version followed later that year. That project was built for public engagement and recruitment. The new Mirage simulators are intended for the training of serving pilots.
In 2025, Threye also made a first-of-its-kind demonstration of a fighter and an uncrewed combat aircraft carrying out a paired mission. The demonstration drew on Air Combat Intelligence Development, or ACID, an initiative associated with its parent company, NewSpace. The idea is to develop the intelligence and coordination needed for a piloted fighter to work with an autonomous aircraft during an air combat mission.
That connection makes the Mirage contract part of a larger shift for the group. NewSpace has made significant inroads into military drone programmes, including work to develop an Indian collaborative combat aircraft, or CCA, for the Indian Navy designed to operate alongside piloted fighters. Its projects also include the Sheshnaag attack drone and other systems for the armed forces. For Threye, the new contract brings its experience in digital air combat missions back to the Mirage 2000, the fighter it first put on a computer screen more than a decade ago.
Threye’s Anurag Rana has written for Livefist before and been an art contributor.

work-careers-365d20eaf3.headline: H-1B registrations by Indian IT firms plunge 92% for FY27
work-careers-365d20eaf3.fulltext:
The sharp fall in H-1B registrations by Indian IT firms for FY27 signals that higher immigration costs are reshaping their US staffing strategies, pushing companies towards local hiring and offshore delivery.
On September 19, US President Donald Trump issued a proclamation titled “Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers”, under which certain H-1B petitions filed on or after September 21 are subject to an additional $100,000 payment as a condition of eligibility. USCIS said that petitioners that relied heavily on prospective H-1B beneficiaries seeking consular notification and admission from outside the US in the FY26 cap did not participate in the FY27 H-1B cap registration process in the same manner.
H-1B registrations plunge among Indian IT firms
A USCIS regulatory filing observed, “In many cases, petition volumes even increased as fees rose, suggesting employers view the fees as a necessary cost for accessing foreign talent. Following implementation of the $100,000 Proclamation payment in September 2025, USCIS observed a short-term shock decline of more than 90% in consular H-1B receipts.”
According to USCIS data, for top Indian IT companies — Infosys, TCS, HCL America, LTM, Tech Mahindra and Wipro — H-1B registrations for the FY27 cap fell to 1,763 from 21,919 in FY26, a decline of about 92%.
Infosys saw registrations fall from 8,886 in FY26 to 759 in FY27, a 91.5% decline. TCS registrations dropped 95.2% from 5,955 to 284, while HCL America fell 90% from 3,855 to 387. LTM’s registrations fell 85.3% from 1,211 to 178, while Tech Mahindra Americas fell 95.8% from 1,027 to 43. Wipro’s registrations fell 88.6% from 985 to 112.
Decline extends to other large employers
The decline was not limited to Indian IT companies. Among the other large employers listed, IBM’s registrations fell 95.6% from 2,855 to 126, while Accenture’s dropped 94% from 1,324 to 79. Capgemini’s registrations fell 87.5% from 1,703 to 213. However, the decline was less pronounced at several large US technology companies. Microsoft’s registrations fell 31.8% from 3,640 to 2,481, and Apple’s declined 16.3% from 2,705 to 2,265.
“The decline reflects a combination of cost, policy, and business-model factors. The $100,000 payment on new H-1B petitions has changed the economics of sending entry-level and mid-level talent to the US, particularly for services contracts priced on tight margins. The move towards a wage-weighted selection process further favours higher-salaried, specialised roles, which do not match the typical profile of large deployment programmes,” Lakshmi Iyer, Chief Client Officer & Chairperson, StudyIn India, echoed.
IT firms build local hiring and offshore capabilities
Leading IT services firms have spent several years building local US hiring pipelines, campus partnerships and delivery centres, reducing their dependence on new visas.
According to TCS’ FY26 annual report, the company is pursuing diversified sourcing and local hiring strategies, with greater emphasis on hiring local talent and building STEM capabilities locally to reduce its dependence on work visas materially.
Infosys’ FY26 annual report notes that the company has established innovation hubs, nearshore centres and digital design studios across geographies.
Moreover, as per its annual reports, in FY26, Tech Mahindra had 112,609 employees, or 80.31% of its workforce, based offshore, while 27,607 employees, or 19.69%, were onsite. In FY25, 110,958 employees (79.67% of the workforce) were offshore, while 28,313 employees (20.33%) were onsite.
Firms explore alternative staffing models
Iyer explained that for Indian IT services firms, H-1B has historically supported a volume-driven model, with professionals deployed to client sites across multiple projects. A fixed $100,000 cost weighs far more heavily on such roles than on the specialised, higher-paid positions that global technology companies typically sponsor, often for their own product and research teams. Wage-weighted selection widens the same gap. Global firms also tend to hire graduates already studying in the US, where the visa is one step in a longer talent pipeline.
Onsite presence remains important for client-facing roles, but work at US client locations is declining as firms rely more on local hires, selective short-term India-based deployments and offshore delivery. Mature remote collaboration and India’s GCC ecosystem, along with immigration constraints, are accelerating this shift.
She added that nearshore centres in Canada, Mexico and other Latin American markets offer time-zone alignment for clients that need closer collaboration. “On the visa side, firms may lean more on the L-1 intra-company transfer for existing employees, while the O-1 category suits a small pool of highly specialised professionals. Short business visits for meetings and workshops will also continue to support client engagement,” Iyer shared.

health-tech-af6d4469b8.headline: US 100% Pharma Tariff: Select Indian Specialty Drugs Get Zero Duty
health-tech-af6d4469b8.fulltext:
The US has set a zero tariff on a defined set of specialty drugs from India and 19 other jurisdictions, even as its 100% pharmaceutical duty began applying to more companies on September 29.
Pharma stocks gained while the broader market fell. But the relief is narrower than the headline suggests, and the question that matters for investors is how much of each Indian drugmaker’s US portfolio sits inside the exempt categories.
The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) defined the eligible products and listed India among 20 eligible jurisdictions in a notice published in the Federal Register on September 23 (91 FR 60360).
How the 100% Pharma Tariff Works
Proclamation 11020, issued on April 2, 2026, imposed a 100% ad valorem tariff under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act on certain patented pharmaceuticals and associated ingredients.
According to the BIS notice, it took effect on July 31 for companies listed in Annexe III of the proclamation and on September 29 for all other companies. Lower rates apply to products from certain jurisdictions and to companies with Commerce-approved onshoring agreements.
Which Specialty Drugs Get Zero Tariff
The zero rate covers drugs and ingredients where all approved indications are designated orphan, nuclear medicines, plasma-derived therapies, fertility drugs, cell therapy products, gene therapy products, antibody-drug conjugates, medical countermeasures for chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear threats, and animal health products.
A product qualifies through one of two routes, the notice says: it comes from a jurisdiction with a current or forthcoming trade and security framework agreement with the US, or Commerce determines it meets an urgent US health need.
Besides India, the eligible jurisdictions are Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, the European Union, Guatemala, Indonesia, Japan, Jordan, Malaysia, North Macedonia, South Korea, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Taiwan, Thailand, the United Kingdom and Vietnam. The notice says changes to the list may be published in a future notice.
Generics Remain Outside The Tariff Regime
Business Standard reported that the Commerce notice says generic pharmaceutical products and their associated ingredients are not covered by the Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs. Generics are therefore not currently subject to the duty.
Why The Impact On Indian Drugmakers Is Narrower Than It Looks
The US is India’s largest pharma export market. Shipments there fell nearly 10% year on year to $9.47 billion in FY26, over 30% of total pharma exports, Business Standard reported, citing Pharmexcil data compiled from DGCI&S figures. Indian drugmakers also supplied nearly half of US generic prescriptions in 2022, according to IQVIA data cited by Reuters.
Because generics already sit outside the tariff, the exemption matters for the narrower set of Indian-made specialty products within its scope, not for the bulk of the US generics business.
How Pharma Stocks Moved On September 29
Pharma outperformed a falling market. Business Standard reported in the morning trade that the Nifty Pharma index rose more than 1% while the Nifty 50 fell about 0.55%. Upstox, citing NSE data, put the index’s intraday high at 27,032.40, up 1.01%. Moneycontrol later showed it up at 0.6%.
Moneycontrol reported that Dr Reddy’s Laboratories rose more than 2% to a one-month high of ₹1,247.70, heading for a third straight session of gains and up nearly 4% over the period. Mankind Pharma gained more than 4.5% and was the top gainer across the Nifty 200 and Nifty 500.
Sun Pharma rose nearly 1% and Cipla 0.3%. Lupin and Zydus Lifesciences also traded higher in early trade, Business Upturn data showed.
The exemption was not the only supportive factor. Business Standard quoted an analyst who also pointed to a weak rupee and fewer regulatory warning letters. Business Today noted the Nifty Pharma index is up about 18% this year, while the Sensex is down about 13%.
Dr Reddy’s, Lupin And Zydus: What To Check
Moneycontrol named all three as companies expected to benefit because of their specialty pharmaceutical presence.
The notice defines product categories, not companies, so the earnings effect depends on three company-level facts: which of their US products fall in the exempt categories, how much revenue those products generate, and whether they would otherwise have faced the 100% duty.
The uneven intraday moves across pharma stocks underline that the tariff treatment will not affect every company in the same way.
What To Watch Next
Company commentary on qualifying products and the US revenue mix, in upcoming results and earnings calls, is the first test. The BIS notice also lets companies submit product-specific requests for zero-tariff treatment on urgent US health need grounds on an ongoing basis from September 23, and says the eligible jurisdiction list may change in a future notice.
For broader market context, track institutional flows on NiftyTrader’s FII-DII Tracker: https://niftytrader.in/fii-dii-data
Bottom Line
The 100% tariff is the headline, but the exemption is product-specific: zero duty for defined specialty categories from eligible jurisdictions, with generics already outside the regime. For Indian drugmakers, the impact will vary with how much of the US portfolio falls in the exempt categories, and company disclosures will settle that.

world-6f004bb8a0.headline: Estonia blames Russia for arson attack on drone maker supplying Ukraine
world-6f004bb8a0.fulltext:
European and Nato leaders have expressed full support for Estonia and Ukraine after the Baltic state said an August arson attack on a drone manufacturer supplying Kyiv was an act of sabotage commissioned by Moscow’s security services.
Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, said on social media on Tuesday that such attacks were “absolutely unacceptable” and that Russia’s chargé d’affaires in the Estonian capital, Tallinn, was being summoned to his ministry.
Estonia’s national security agency said a fire broke out on 15 August at a building in Tallinn used by Milrem Robotics, which makes unmanned ground vehicles used in Ukraine. Two Latvian suspects were detained in Latvia on 17 August, followed by a third the next day. All three were handed over to Estonia, it said.
Tsahkna said the subsequent investigation had led authorities to “conclude with certainty” that the attack was “an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation”. It was part of a “broader campaign across Europe aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine”, he said.
Estonia’s prime minister, Kristen Michal, said his country’s response to Russia’s campaign would “be the opposite: stronger security at home, more support for Ukraine and greater pressure on Russia. We will not be intimidated.”
Estonia has repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid provocations since the beginning of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and, along with its fellow Baltic states Latvia and Lithuania, has significantly increased its defence spending.
Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said Estonia’s allegations were “unfounded, ill-considered, absolutely not reflecting the reality, not containing any substantiation whatsoever”. He said Russia “cannot take such statements seriously, and we won’t”.
Western allies pledged their continued support to Estonia and Ukraine. Speaking in Brussels, Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, said Russia “continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies”, adding that it was “failing … on the battlefield in Ukraine, and failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine”.
Speaking alongside Rutte, Lithuania’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said Russia’s actions were becoming “increasingly hostile and less restrained … We see the hybrid attacks – in Lithuania, Poland, Germany, elsewhere. And it’s not a question of proximity now, it’s a question of Russia’s actions.”
Lithuania’s foreign minister, Kęstutis Budrys, said Russia’s fingerprints were “all over” the Tallinn attack, while the Latvian president, Edgars Rinkēvičs, said further support for Ukraine “will be needed, and must be provided”.
The EU said it stood with Estonia, describing the arson attack as “reckless” and saying it would not be put off supporting Ukraine. “Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. This will not happen,” a European Commission spokesperson said.
France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, called the arson attack a “dangerous escalation”. Moscow “needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine”, Macron said on social media.
Sweden’s acting prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, called Estonia’s formal attribution of the attack “extremely serious”, and Britain’s ambassador to Estonia, Jo Lomas, said the UK “stands with Estonia in confronting these unacceptable attacks. They will not weaken our resolve or our support for Ukraine.”
About 200 incidents of suspected Russian sabotage and malign activity have been recorded across Europe since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, including arson plots at warehouses, drone incursions, thefts of defence technology and cyber-attacks on essential European infrastructure.
Agence France-Presse and Associated Press contributed to this report

ai-007dd370ab.headline: OpenAI announces ‘dots’ agent after scrapping launch of new AI model over safety concerns
ai-007dd370ab.fulltext:
Less than 24 hours after OpenAI announced it would scrap the launch of an artificial intelligence model over safety concerns, the company debuted a whole new suite of AI tools.
During its annual showcase for developers in San Francisco on Tuesday, Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, enthusiastically unveiled an AI agent called “dots” that he said was “more ambitious” than ChatGPT and a “whole new way to work with AI”.
“It’s like an AI helper that always has your back,” Altman said, to loud applause from the developers attending the event. “In the future, if you like, you can work with a whole team of dots.”
OpenAI’s dots are colorful little blobs, donning berets or glasses, that appear on people’s phones or laptops, can be integrated into other apps and can follow commands. The agents can perform tasks without supervision such as schedule a meeting, book a flight or dole out assignments to colleagues. OpenAI says the “dots are an extension of you” and describes the tool as “frontier intelligence”.
Dots are powered by GPT-6 Astra, the company’s latest model. OpenAI said the previous evening it would halt the release of GPT-6.1 Astra because the updated model showed deceptive behavior during testing.
OpenAI’s dots will compete with Meta’s new AI agent, Muse, released two weeks ago. Meta’s product is aimed at everyday consumers more so than business customers, as OpenAI’s is, though Meta announced a small business offering Tuesday. The agent’s app, available in the US, has been downloaded more than 3m times.
OpenAI also apologized on Monday for one of its AI agents going rogue and hacking an Australian government website. The apology came after the company has been plagued by reports and admissions that its AI systems have been acting independently and gaining access to various company and government websites.
During OpenAI’s event on Tuesday, Altman touted the power of Astra and introduced similar potent AI tools. One model, called GPT-6.1 Sol, is cheaper and “smarter than Astra in many ways”, the CEO said. Altman also previewed a new “Ultrafast” mode for its AI coding models, which can generate outputs up to eight times faster than what’s available now.
“People often talk about AI as a new industrial revolution, I find that quite off-putting,” Altman said at the end of his presentation. “There are some parts of life that we cannot and should not automate. I believe that the future, if we get this right, can be more like a new Renaissance than a new industrial revolution.”

world-a2a8510859.headline: Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons
world-a2a8510859.fulltext:
Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons
- Published
Chinese AI developer Moonshot is conducting an internal review after researchers were able to persuade two of its popular Kimi models to tell them how to make biological weapons and carry out assassinations.
Mindgard, which tests the security of AI systems, told the BBC it discovered in July that Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm could evade safety limits put in place by developers.
It arose during a process called "jailbreaking", where researchers use a series of complex instructions to see if AI tools ignore guardrails - which Mindgard said should have stopped Kimi from discussing concerning topics.
Moonshot told the BBC it welcomed third-party input "as a key pillar for building better and safer AI".
The company also told the BBC it was in discussion with Mindgard about its findings.
Mindgard's founder Peter Garraghan told the BBC World Service programme Tech Life that its findings about Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm were concerning.
"Once the jailbreak works it will talk about any topic, it will even freely offer up recommendations about other topics that are also nefarious and it will be inventive and creative," he said.
Jailbreaks present a different kind of risk to those seen with the recent slew of high-profile AI incidents.
These have seen autonomous AI tools known as agents, developed by US firms including OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic, hack some online services.
While jailbreaks are complex processes that can take a lot of time and determination some experts fear hackers and other bad actors could try to use them to cause harm.
Anthropic recently said it had identified and disrupted attempts to use one of its AI model for "malicious activity" that could support the development of biological weapons.
Cyber-attack launchpad
Mindgard has not proven whether the answers supplied by Kimi on concerning topics would work.
But it argued guardrails should have prevented the models in question from entering into discussion with users on such subjects.
The firm said it was also confident a jailbroken Kimi 2.6 could allow hackers to run code on its computing resources and connect to the internet - making it a potential launchpad for cyber-attacks.
Garraghan defended Mindgard's decision to publicly discuss its jailbreak of Moonshot's systems, saying it had informed the developer and was not revealing key details about how it got the firm's models to ignore guardrails.
Mindgard alerted Moonshot to the jailbreak in an email on 27 July, following up about a week later.
It then published a blog about the issue on 12 September.
But the company said Moonshot only made contact recently, after it was approached by the BBC for comment.
In part of an email to Mindgard asking for more details, shared with the BBC by Moonshot, it said its model had generally shown "a high refusal rate for these types of requests" in internal evaluations.
- What is AI, how does it work and why are some people concerned about it? 
  - Published14 September
Preventing jailbreaks
The findings come as the AI industry continues to be split on whether closed, proprietary models - like those powering ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude systems - or open-source tools are the best or safest way forward.
Kimi is an open-weight model, meaning someone could in theory take the model and run it themselves on their own computing infrastructure.
Prof Alan Woodward, of the University of Surrey, told the BBC there was a risk open-source models might end up in the wrong hands, but they could also be harnessed for cyber-defence.
He noted that AI firm Hugging Face used a Chinese open-source model to understand a hack later revealed to have been carried out by OpenAI agents.
Prof Woodward said international regulation was unlikely to match the pace of AI development, saying: "It's taken us decades to agree on the format of telephone numbers."
Like Mindgard founder Garraghan, Prof Woodward believes there should be a greater focus on identifying and prosecuting humans who misuse AI.

climate-energy-b17b79c040.headline: India’s Solar Manufacturing Boom Faces US Trade Headwinds: Report
climate-energy-b17b79c040.fulltext:
India’s solar manufacturing capacity has expanded rapidly, with 242.7 GW of operating module capacity by Q2 2026, according to Rhodium Group’s Clean Investment Monitor. The report said India’s large domestic market could help absorb additional supply as US trade measures create challenges for Indian solar exports.
Key Highlights
- India’s operating solar module capacity reached 242.7 GW by Q2 2026.
- Solar manufacturing investment has accelerated sharply in recent years.
- India’s domestic market could help absorb additional solar manufacturing output.
- US trade measures are creating export challenges for Indian solar manufacturers.
New Delhi, Sept 29: India’s solar manufacturing industry has expanded rapidly in recent years, with the country emerging as a major manufacturing base even as new US trade measures create challenges for exports. The latest Clean Investment Monitor from Rhodium Group shows that India’s share of global solar manufacturing investment has increased significantly, while domestic manufacturing capacity continues to expand.
According to the report, India had 242.7 GW of operating solar module capacity by Q2 2026, compared with 40.5 GW of cell capacity and 2.5 GW of wafer capacity. The figures highlight the rapid expansion of downstream module manufacturing, while also pointing to a significant gap between module and upstream cell and wafer production. Rhodium Group said recent investment announcements indicate that this gap could gradually narrow, with announced cell and wafer capacity increasing substantially.
The report noted that India’s solar manufacturing expansion has been supported by policies requiring the use of domestically manufactured solar equipment through the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) framework. The country is also seeing greater investment in upstream manufacturing, including cells, wafers and polysilicon. Rhodium said announced wafer capacity increased to 24 GW by Q2 2026, while announced cell capacity rose to 39.3 GW and announced polysilicon capacity reached 10 GW.
At the same time, Indian solar manufacturers face pressure from the US market. The US Department of Commerce announced final affirmative determinations in September 2026 in anti-dumping and countervailing duty investigations covering crystalline silicon photovoltaic cells from India and other countries. The measures add to the trade barriers facing Indian manufacturers seeking access to the US market.
Rhodium Group has previously noted that preliminary US trade measures had effectively restricted Indian solar exports to the US, while domestic manufacturers were also dealing with excess downstream capacity. Its latest analysis said India’s large domestic market provides an alternative demand base, although manufacturers could face pressure on margins as they adjust to changing export conditions. The report also noted that India’s solar manufacturing investment rose sharply relative to other markets, making the country an increasingly important location for global clean-technology manufacturing.
India’s expanding domestic solar market and growing manufacturing ecosystem provide an important demand base for the industry, while manufacturers face the need to diversify export markets and strengthen upstream production amid changing global trade conditions.

india-66cf3fca4f.headline: Apple Pay set to launch in India with Axis Bank today, sources say
india-66cf3fca4f.fulltext:
Apple is set to launch Apple Pay in India later Tuesday with Axis Bank as its initial banking partner, TechCrunch has learned, bringing its payments service to the world’s most populous country after years on the sidelines of a market dominated by UPI.
The initial rollout will be limited, according to people familiar with the matter. Apple Pay will initially support eligible Axis Bank cards on Visa and Mastercard, but not India’s homegrown RuPay network. Acceptance will also be restricted to merchants and payment terminals that have been enabled for the service.
Unlike India’s ubiquitous Unified Payments Interface (UPI) system, which lets consumers make instant bank-to-bank payments without relying on cards, Apple Pay is card-based and requires individual issuers and payment infrastructure providers to integrate with the service. This makes a broad rollout more complex. Apple’s commercial terms have also emerged as a sticking point with some of India’s largest banks, the people said.
Apple is seeking a fee of about 20 basis points on transactions, according to the people, a significant bite out of the roughly 40 to 50 basis points of margin in the payments layer. The fee structure is broadly consistent with Apple Pay’s commercial model in other markets, the people said. HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, and SBI Card are not expected to support Apple Pay at launch as negotiations over commercial terms continue, one of the people told TechCrunch.
Apple, Axis Bank, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, and SBI Card did not respond to requests for comment. Earlier this month, Reuters reported that Apple was preparing to launch Apple Pay in India in October, starting with Axis Bank credit cards.
Apple Pay is entering a payments market that looks markedly different from the U.S. and other card-heavy economies. India’s digital payments boom has been driven largely by UPI, the state-backed system that lets consumers move money directly between bank accounts.
UPI handles the bulk of digital payments in India, where scanning a QR code to pay directly from a bank account has become commonplace. Apple Pay, by contrast, will initially address a much smaller card payments market.
Nevertheless, Apple Pay could appeal to India’s growing base of iPhone users, who tend to be more affluent and are more likely to use premium credit cards. Those customers could make the service hard for banks to ignore, despite UPI’s dominance.
Even if Apple Pay remains a niche service, the economics could still make India meaningful for Apple. The transaction fee the iPhone maker would charge would give it another way to monetize its growing base of iPhone users in the country, the people said.
At launch, eligible Axis Bank customers will be allowed to add their credit cards to Apple’s Wallet app and use Apple Pay for online purchases as well as contactless payments at supported terminals, the people said.
An Apple Pay transaction could work at a terminal operated by an independent payments provider that has enabled the service but fail at another terminal whose acquiring bank has not, one of the people said. That could make acceptance uneven during the initial rollout, even for customers with supported cards.
The launch adds another piece to Apple’s growing business in India, where it has been expanding iPhone sales, local manufacturing, and its retail footprint. Apple accounted for 28% of India’s smartphone market by value in 2025, up from 23% a year earlier, per an earlier report by Counterpoint Research.
India already accounts for about a quarter of global iPhone production, and that share could rise to 30% to 35% over the next five years, Indian English daily Business Standard reported last month, citing an Indian government official.

india-141fb6930e.headline: A Misguided Tech Solution is Putting India's Electoral Integrity at Risk
india-141fb6930e.fulltext:
A Misguided Tech Solution is Putting India's Electoral Integrity at Risk
Amber Sinha / Sep 29, 2026
Amber Sinha is a contributing editor at Tech Policy Press.
A mounting controversy surrounding efforts to technically centralize and deduplicate India’s electoral rolls reached new heights last week with the revelation that the Election Commission of India (ECI) repeatedly overrode the formal objections of two election commissioners, who saw “unauthorized” and “illegal” handling of voter records.
The scandal is fast emerging as a political crisis for the Modi Government in a difficult year.
Dissent notes filed by the election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, between Oct. 2025 and Aug. 2026 against the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, raise serious questions about the undemocratic functioning of one of India’s most protected institutions, which handles numerous local elections in any given year. 
While internal bureaucratic friction is not entirely new within statutory bodies, the substance of these objections is alarming. It shines a light on trends within India’s electoral management that have been previously discussed on Tech Policy Press here (2024) and here (2025): the technological centralization of digital electoral infrastructure.
For some years, the Indian state has been captivated by the allure of techno-solutionism. There is a widely shared belief that complex socio-political challenges can be neatly resolved through digital databases and algorithmic engineering. Within the context of electoral management, we have seen this manifest previously in the “purification” of electoral rolls, undertaken in limited, albeit devastating, ways. As for instance, when the National Electoral Roll Purification and Authentication Programme (NERPAP) sought to link voter IDs with biometric Aadhaar ID data to weed out duplicates in 2015. Before the Supreme Court intervened, this centralized, algorithmic matching resulted in the deletion of millions of voters without due process, disproportionately affecting marginalized communities whose digital legibility is often fraught.
The current update of the electoral rolls—the Special Intensive Revision (SIR)—began in 2025 and does not merely repeat these past mistakes; it takes the ideology of database ‘purification’ to its logical, unchecked conclusion. By shifting the locus of control away from local administrations and into a centralized software architecture, the ECI has effectively hardcoded disenfranchisement into its processes.
How the ECINet works
The key technological product in this shift is the ECINet portal introduced in January 2026. Historically, the strength and resilience of India’s electoral machinery have relied heavily on its federated, decentralized nature. Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) and Booth Level Officers (BLOs) are the backbone of this system. They possess the vital, granular, contextual knowledge necessary to verify voter status on the ground. When discrepancies arise, these local officials conduct physical verifications, hold hearings, and make nuanced administrative decisions based on lived realities rather than rigid database parameters.
The centralization of ECINet circumvents these time-established practices. As highlighted this week by an investigation of The Indian Express on voter deletion in Goa due to the SIR, the software architecture itself has begun to override the statutory powers of local officials. In Goa, following a local outcry over arbitrary voter deletions, state EROs conducted hearings and determined that several previously deleted voters were, in fact, eligible citizens who still resided at their registered addresses. However, when these ground-level officials attempted to reinstate the voters, they found their hands tied by the digital interface. The centralized ECINet software provided no functionality for EROs to restore names to the electoral rolls.
This incident in Goa is a textbook example of the techno-determinism at the heart of India’s digital governance practices. The software’s architecture—controlled from the capital city New Delhi—dictated the boundaries of administrative action on the ground in Goa. Code, in this instance, literally became law. When a centralized IT system makes central control the default, it functionally strips local administrators of their legal authority and forces people to bear the burdensome cost of filing entirely new voter registration applications. It is a system designed for the convenience of centralized database management, entirely divorced from the friction and reality of human democracy.
Overriding administrative friction
The dissolution of localized responsiveness poses a severe threat to electoral integrity. A robust democratic system requires administrative friction—mechanisms for appeal, human review, and contextual judgment. Centralized technological systems, however, optimize for frictionless scale. When millions of names are processed through opaque deduplication algorithms and centralized portals, the inevitable errors scale just as rapidly. As former Chief Election Commissioner O.P. Rawat publicly warned this week, massive numbers of eligible voters are at risk of losing their constitutional right to vote, simply because they fail to meet the rigid, binary criteria of a centralized database.
The fallout over SIR is already reshaping the electoral landscape. The over-reliance on centralized digital infrastructure has created widespread on-the-ground chaos. Voters are finding their names arbitrarily struck off the rolls due to backend ‘data cleaning’ exercises. The fundamental burden of proof has shifted as citizens are no longer presumed eligible to vote until proven otherwise by a local BLO.
By consolidating control over the ECINet software, the upper echelons of the Electoral Commission effectively bypass the scrutiny and contextual knowledge of state-level officials. It is precisely this bypassing of established checks and balances that prompted the unprecedented dissent notes from within the Commission itself. When structural changes to the digital infrastructure that governs the voting rights of over a billion people are implemented unilaterally, the very foundations of institutional accountability are eroded.
The public uproar over the SIR controversy indicates a growing awareness of the dangers of algorithmic governance in the electoral sphere. Recognizing the existential threat posed by these opaque processes, over 2,000 citizens, civil society members, and legal experts recently wrote an open letter to the Chief Justice of India, urging the Supreme Court to stay the SIR and initiate suo motu proceedings on the ECI's conduct. This collective action underscores a critical truth: the management of digital electoral rolls is not a benign IT project, but an active site of constitutional contestation.
Moving forward, the policy discourse surrounding India’s elections must pivot away from a blind faith in techno-solutionism. The ECI must abandon its trajectory toward absolute database centralization. Digital tools should be deployed to augment and assist the human judgment of local EROs and BLOs, not to render them obsolete. If we fail to challenge the techno-determinism driving the centralization of the ECI, we risk cementing an electoral system where the constitutional right to vote is no longer guaranteed by law, but dictated by the rigid, opaque logic of a centralized database.

Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI
- Published
US President Donald Trump has ruled out any sort of joint venture with China in artificial intelligence (AI), arguing it would be tantamount to "giving away secrets" to America's main economic rival.
Speaking at an event in Washington on Tuesday, Trump again argued against putting any restrictions on the technology that would stifle growth in the future, despite mounting public concern.
Following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House last week, Beijing and Washington announced the launch of a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for November.
The two countries also established a new communications channel to prevent misunderstandings during AI-related incidents.
During Tuesday's event marking the launch of America.gov - a new AI-powered website designed to streamline government services - Trump argued the US was "leading by a lot" in the AI sector and did not want to "mix it up" with potential competitors.
"If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said. "Frankly, there is nobody in third place...it's all between us and China."
Trump added that while the topic of AI came up during his meeting with President Xi last week, he remained steadfast against any sort of joint cooperation to develop the technology.
"Then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know," he said, remarking that "we're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way".
Prior to Trump's meeting with Xi, China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hindered AI governance.
At a later White House lunch with representatives of government agencies and technology companies - including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta - Trump said among those present, there was "a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation".
Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Trump said that the technology leaders had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from the potential hazards of AI.
A "Super Intelligence Czar" would likely be named in the coming days, Trump added. The president signed an executive order, external on Tuesday afternoon that will formally change the name of AI to "Super Intelligence" in government documents.
Domestically, Trump has faced increasing public concern over the potential dangers of AI and calls for additional guardrails to be put in place.
A recent poll published by Politico in late September found that two of every three Americans believes there is at least a "moderate" risk that AI could destroy humanity.
A significant portion of Trump supporters polled - 44% - said they would prefer if AI development could be paused.
The US president, however, has repeatedly shrugged off safety concerns, referring to them as a "hoax" and comparing them to the "global warming scam" he claims is "being perpetrated by radical left Dumocrats".

work-careers-3cafec1d4d.fulltext:
India's global capability centre (GCC) sector is undergoing a significant workforce transition, with job cut estimates ranging from 5,000 to as many as 30,000 roles this year as organisations pursue AI-led productivity gains and restructure operating models.
According to a report by Moneycontrol, the reductions are taking place even as GCCs continue to expand their strategic responsibilities across technology, engineering, artificial intelligence and product development. The trend highlights a shift away from broad-based hiring towards leaner teams with deeper technical expertise.
The development comes at a time when India remains the world's largest GCC destination, employing an estimated 2.4 million to 2.5 million professionals across more than 2,100 centres.
Wide variation in layoff estimates
Industry experts cited by Moneycontrol have offered differing assessments of the scale of workforce reductions.
Pareekh Jain, CEO of EIIRTrend, estimated that GCCs may have cut between 25,000 and 30,000 jobs this year. Meanwhile, Sameer Dhanrajani, CEO of 3AI, placed the figure significantly lower at around 4,000 to 5,000 roles.
Reported workforce reductions include:
- Around 200 jobs at PayPal
- Approximately 1,500 roles at Visa
- Workforce cuts at ServiceNow
- Reductions across several other GCC operations
While estimates vary, industry observers broadly agree that hiring priorities are changing as organisations seek greater efficiency through automation and AI-enabled workflows.
AI is reshaping how work is organised
The workforce changes are occurring alongside a broader transformation in the nature of work performed within GCCs.
Data cited by Moneycontrol indicates:
- 17.7% of GCC work is classified as commodity-based
- 38.1% of work is categorised as complex
- Around 55% of work portfolios have some exposure to potential AI displacement
Industry experts note that exposure to AI displacement does not imply equivalent job losses. Instead, it suggests that specific tasks within roles could be automated, redesigned or augmented through AI technologies.
As organisations deploy generative AI, automation tools and intelligent workflows, routine activities are increasingly being streamlined, changing the mix of skills required across teams.
Strategic value continues to rise
Despite workforce reductions in certain areas, GCCs are continuing to gain prominence within multinational organisations.
According to the report, centres in India are taking on larger mandates in:
- Artificial intelligence
- Software engineering
- Product development
- Enterprise platforms
- Technology innovation
Many of these responsibilities were previously concentrated at global headquarters or regional hubs outside India.
This shift means workforce size and strategic importance are no longer moving in parallel. A GCC may employ fewer people in some functions while assuming greater responsibility for critical products, platforms and AI systems.
A new phase for India's GCC ecosystem
The latest workforce adjustments underline a broader evolution within India's GCC landscape.
For more than a decade, growth was often measured through large-scale hiring and rapid headcount expansion. Today, organisations appear increasingly focused on productivity, automation and specialised expertise.
While some roles are being eliminated or redesigned, companies continue to establish new GCCs and recruit for niche technical positions. The result is a more selective hiring environment where advanced skills and business impact are becoming more important than workforce scale alone.
As AI adoption accelerates across global enterprises, India's GCC sector appears set to enter a new phase where capability depth, innovation and specialised talent define growth more than headcount expansion.

agritech-f88f4ac3eb.headline: Why first monsoon drought in 11 years left India dry, and wet
agritech-f88f4ac3eb.fulltext:
Despite a late burst of heavy rain, the 2026 southwest monsoon is shaping up to be India’s driest in 11 years. Last week’s deep depression brought widespread rain to parts of east, northeast, central and north India, cutting the season’s deficit from 15% to around 12% in a span of four-five days. But the monsoon is still set to be India’s first deficient season since 2015 and among the 10 weakest monsoons since Independence.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) classifies a seasonal rainfall deficit of 10% or more as ‘deficient’, its lowest rainfall category, commonly described as a monsoon drought.
The significance of this year’s rainfall deficit becomes clearer against the recent past. Five of the last seven monsoons produced either excess or above-normal rainfall. India appeared to have entered a relatively wet phase in its multi-decadal monsoon cycle, marked by fewer droughts.
This year has broken that run, with El Niño playing a major role. El Niño is the periodic warming of surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific that alters atmospheric circulation around the globe. The 2026 event is developing into the strongest on record.
“A clear way of identifying if El Niño has affected the monsoon is by checking whether the monsoon wind circulation has weakened,” says Roxy Mathew Koll, climate scientist at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. 
“This year, there was a marked weakening of these winds, which was evident right from monsoon’s onset.”
The monsoon reached Kerala on June 4, just three days after the normal date, and initially advanced rapidly. By June 8, it covered much of southern India; by June 12, the northeast and much of eastern India were under monsoon winds. Then it stalled for nearly two weeks, reaching northwest India only in the first week of July.
With monsoon winds weak even where the system had arrived, June ended with a countrywide rainfall deficit of more than 35%, the highest in 12 years.
Bay of Bengal lows on a high
The weakness persisted through the following months, but another feature of the monsoon changed: low-pressure systems (LPS) began repeatedly forming over the Bay of Bengal and moving inland, transporting moisture and producing heavy rain.
There were no such systems in June, but four in July, six in August and three in September, including the deep depression that crossed the north Andhra-south Odisha coast on September 23-24. Thirteen LPS during these three months is above the normal 10-11.
The impact is visible on the district rainfall map. A swathe of relatively good rainfall runs from parts of Rajasthan through Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Gangetic West Bengal and Odisha. This is broadly the corridor through which many of the LPS travelled.
Odisha, impacted by nearly all of these systems, witnessed its wettest monsoon in 20 years. This year’s June-September rainfall of over 1,480mm is among the highest five the state has experienced since 1901.
“When the monsoon is less organised, like this year, low-pressure systems play a much more dominant role,” Koll says. “Even though, on the large scale, El Niño’s effect on the monsoon was strong, these smaller weather systems were bringing in rain, even extreme rainfall. Had these systems been absent, the monsoon deficit may have been 20% or higher.”
Western disturbances, moist weather systems moving into north India from the Mediterranean region, also remained unusually active, just as in recent years. Experts link this trend to climate change. At times, these WDs interacted with LPS, producing extreme rainfall, particularly in the Himalayan states.
The result is a strikingly uneven monsoon. As of September 25, 43% of India’s districts had received deficient or scanty rainfall, with most of the rainfall-starved districts concentrated in four broad clusters. Each of these clusters tells a story.
East and northeast: Driest on record
The East and Northeast region — comprising the seven subdivisions of Bihar, Jharkhand, Gangetic West Bengal, North Bengal and Sikkim, Assam and Meghalaya, Arunachal Pradesh, and the other northeastern states of Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram and Tripura — is heading for its driest monsoon since records began in 1901.
As of September 27, the region had received 1,014.7mm against a normal 1,347mm, a deficit of nearly 25%. Even with the late-season rains, it will remain well below the previous record low of 1,069mm, set in 2013.
The decline is not confined to this year. IMD data shows that average monsoon rainfall in the region since 2000 is about 15% lower than during 1981-2000, and 26% below the peak reached during 1941-1960.
That is a substantial climatic shift, with potential implications for land use and ecology. Yet even during this exceptionally dry monsoon, parts of Assam and Nagaland suffered severe flooding. Experts have pointed to deforestation and development-related changes as factors that magnified the impact of the floods.
Bihar: Five droughts in a row
The most intense concentration of rainfall deficit in eastern India lies across Bihar and adjoining areas of eastern Uttar Pradesh and north Bengal.
As of September 27, 31 of Bihar’s 38 districts were rainfall-deficient. The state is on course for one of its seven driest monsoons since 1901 and is experiencing its fifth consecutive monsoon drought.
A 2024 CEEW (Council on Energy, Environment and Water, a public policy think tank) study of four decades of rainfall data found that during the 1982-2022 period, about 64% of Bihar’s tehsils had experienced declining rainfall in the months of June and July, while 40% recorded a fall of more than 10% across the full four-month monsoon season.
South: Driest in 24 years
The largest rainfall-deficit zone stretches from southern Madhya Pradesh, Vidarbha and Madhya Maharashtra to Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
South India has a rainfall deficit exceeding 23%, making this its driest southwest monsoon since 2002. The district-level picture is starker: 88 of the region’s 147 districts, or 60%, had received deficient or scanty rainfall by September 27.
Rayalaseema in Andhra Pradesh has been particularly badly affected, with a deficit of 38%.
West Rajasthan: A rare desert drought
West Rajasthan, climatologically the country’s driest subdivision, has recorded a rare 31% rainfall deficit. It is the subdivision’s first deficient monsoon in eight years and its lowest seasonal rainfall since 2009.
The contrast with recent decades is striking. In the 17 monsoons since 2009, including 2026, west Rajasthan has averaged 25% above-normal rainfall. It recorded only two deficient seasons, alongside seven excess and two large-excess monsoons.
Punjab: Record wet to deficit
Punjab provides perhaps the sharpest year-to-year contrast. Its rainfall is currently 42% below normal, the largest subdivisional deficit in the country and the state’s worst monsoon since 2004.
Just a year ago, Punjab received 621.6mm, or 41% above normal, its highest monsoon rainfall since 1988. Last year, floods and disease affected paddy yields in the state. This year, deficient rainfall could put both kharif and rabi crops under pressure while adding to the state’s already serious groundwater stress.
Countrywide, the 2026 monsoon may end with a 12-13% shortfall. But more than the deficit, it is a story of a highly uneven monsoon: a weakened large-scale circulation, punctuated by bursts from smaller weather systems, with the result being islands of deluge amid large areas of drought.

opportunities-75e8cd3fc5.fulltext:
FoundrPwr - Building Exceptional Teams ft. Phanindra Sama (RedBus)
Few decisions shape a startup as lastingly as its first twenty hires. Those people set the pace, the standards and the culture that everyone after them inherits. Yet most founders build their early teams through instinct and urgency rather than design.
For the next edition of FoundrPwr, Mela Ventures is hosting Phanindra (Phani) Sama, co-founder and former CEO of redBus, for a conversation on building exceptional teams. 
Phani built redBus from a small team of engineers into a company that led India's online bus ticketing market and became one of the country's earliest notable startup exits. 
He brings an unusually wide view of talent. As an angel investor and advisor, he has watched teams form and grow across many early-stage companies. Through his work in youth skilling, he has also seen how capable professionals are developed from the ground up.
What the conversation will cover
- What distinguishes great early teams, and how founders can assemble one before they have a brand, a large budget or a proven product
- How to attract strong people to an unproven company, and what keeps them there once the early excitement fades
- The practices, norms and structures founders should put in place from the start
- How hiring, leadership and culture need to change as a startup grows from a handful of people into a larger organisation
Who should attend
- Founders of early-stage companies
- Founders making their first key hires or preparing to scale their teams
- Operators and early employees building functions within startups
About the speaker
Phanindra Sama co-founded redBus in 2006 after he could not find a bus ticket home from Bengaluru one Diwali weekend. He led the company as CEO until its acquisition by the ibibo Group in 2013. He later served as Chief Innovation Officer for the Government of Telangana.
Much of Phani's recent work has focused on preparing young people for employment. He co-founded Kakatiya Sandbox, which supports innovation, entrepreneurship and skill development in rural Telangana. He is also closely involved with Deshpande Skilling, which runs residential programmes that train young people for industry roles.
He is currently an Advisor at WestBridge Capital and an angel investor in a number of Indian startups. Phani is an alumnus of BITS Pilani.
Format
5:45 PM: Registration 
6:00 PM: Conversation with Phanindra Sama
7:00 PM: Audience Q&A
7:15 PM: Networking over refreshments
About FoundrPwr and Mela Ventures
FoundrPwr is a founder education series by Mela Ventures. It brings experienced builders and investors into candid conversations on the realities of building a company in India. Mela Ventures is an early-stage venture capital fund based in Bengaluru, investing in B2B companies across Enterprise Technology, DeepTech and ClimateTech. The fund was founded by Krishnakumar Natarajan and Parthasarathy N.S., co-founders of Mindtree.
Seating is limited. Registrations are subject to approval.
